bmt.status_title: Environmental review, ahead of a state adoption
status: The Draft Scope of Work comment period closed on May 8, 2026. A Final Scope of Work follows, listing every comment and how it will be handled in the Environmental Impact Statement.

The city's Office of the Deputy Mayor for Housing, Economic Development and Workforce is the lead agency for review. Once the draft EIS is published, Empire State Development adopts a General Project Plan. The project is proceeding under the State's process rather than the city's ULURP.

The Advisory Task Force continues to meet, and EDC is holding public information sessions on site plan updates. EDC aims to release the first request for proposals for a long term port operator by the end of 2026.
bmt.proposed: A 60 acre all electric port, 6,000 homes of which roughly 2,400 permanently affordable, 275,000 square feet of light industrial space, 250,000 square feet of community facility space, 275,000 square feet of commercial space, a 400 key hotel, and 28 acres of new open space, across 122 acres from Atlantic Avenue to Red Hook. Roughly $3.5 billion, built out into the late 2030s.
bmt.port: EDC asked port operators and maritime businesses how the site could work as a working port, through a Request for Expressions of Interest issued in December 2025. 25 responses came back. EDC has said the environmental review may include a port first alternative for comparison, but that it continues to advance the Vision Plan as approved. The first request for proposals for a long term port operator is expected by the end of 2026.
bmt.background: The Brooklyn Marine Terminal is a 165-acre former port site on the Red Hook waterfront, transferred from the Port Authority to NYCEDC in May 2024. The NYCEDC BMT Vision Plan, completed September 2025, charts a transformation into a modern all-electric port alongside new housing, open space, and community amenities, ending 50 years of disinvestment on the CB6 waterfront.

zones.name: Container & Flex Terminal
zones.text: New 60-acre all-electric marginal pier replaces dilapidated Piers 7 to 10. Handles containers, perishables, cruise, and Blue Highways barge service. Federally funded ($164M USDOT MEGA grant plus $109M City match).

zones.name: Atlantic Basin District
zones.text: BCT, Pier 12, and Pier 11 uplands. Planned for 2,200 housing units (880 affordable), modernized Brooklyn Cruise Terminal, up to 400 hotel keys, 220K sf industrial, 200K sf commercial, and 11 acres of public open space.

zones.name: BMT North
zones.text: Atlantic Ave (N) to Degraw St (S), Columbia St (E) to new neighborhood street (W). 3,800 housing units (1,520 affordable), new public school, 17 acres open space, 55K sf light industrial, 75K sf commercial.

zones.name: Open Space & Greenway
zones.text: Nearly one mile of greenway connecting Brooklyn Bridge Park to the Atlantic Basin. Pier 7 destination park, neighborhood parks, and 5,000+ linear feet of new public waterfront access.

process.name: BMTDC Formation
process.text: Brooklyn Marine Terminal Development Corporation created within 6 weeks of Vision Plan vote to implement commitments and oversee GPP process.

process.name: Empire State Development GPP
process.text: The Vision Plan feeds into ESD's General Project Plan process, which includes environmental review and Public Authorities Control Board final approval.

process.name: Phase 1 (through 2030)
process.text: Simultaneous start of marginal pier construction, 170K sf Pier 11 industrial building, and BMT North housing. Port operator RFP to be released post-GPP.

process.name: Task Force
process.text: 28-member Task Force chaired by Rep. Dan Goldman, co-chaired by Council Member Avilés and State Senator Gounardes. CB6 Board Member Mike Racioppo served as Task Force member.

bmt.source: NYC Economic Development Corporation, BMT Vision Plan, September 2025.

gowanus.title: Gowanus Rezoning
gowanus.subtitle: Approved November 2021, about 82 blocks
gowanus.intro: Zoning determines what can legally be built on specific pieces of land. A rezoning changes what is and isn't allowed. In New York City that requires the applicant to go through the Uniform Land Use Review Procedure, known as ULURP. For Gowanus, New York City was the applicant, and it changed more than 80 mostly industrial blocks into a new mixed-use district with over 9,000 units of housing, including around 3,000 permanently affordable units, along with more than 6 acres of new open space, parkland, and space for artists.

timeline.label: Application Filed
timeline.desc: DCP files application 2018K0382 to begin the Gowanus neighborhood planning study.

timeline.label: CB6 → DCP
timeline.desc: CB6 sends its first letter to DCP as the neighborhood planning study begins.

timeline.label: Bridging Gowanus
timeline.desc: DCP holds community engagement sessions to gather input on the future of the Gowanus neighborhood.

timeline.label: CB6 → DCP
timeline.desc: CB6 submits formal comments to DCP on the Gowanus planning proposal.

timeline.label: CB6 → DCP & Mayor
timeline.desc: CB6 writes to both DCP and the Mayor on the Gowanus rezoning.

timeline.label: Certification Blocked
timeline.desc: Voice of Gowanus files lawsuit. A judge issues a TRO blocking ULURP certification originally planned for Jan 19.

timeline.label: CB6 → DCP
timeline.desc: CB6 writes to DCP during the legal dispute over ULURP certification procedures.

timeline.label: CB6 → DCP
timeline.desc: CB6 sends a follow-up letter to DCP on the rezoning process.

timeline.label: ULURP Certified
timeline.desc: TRO lifted. City Planning Commission certifies the rezoning — officially starting the ULURP clock.

timeline.label: CB6 Public Hearing
timeline.desc: CB6 holds a large hybrid public hearing on the Gowanus Neighborhood Plan.

timeline.label: CB6 Approves
timeline.desc: CB6 Full Board votes 28–6 to approve the rezoning with modifications. Resolution documents CB6's formal position and conditions.

timeline.label: Borough President Approves
timeline.desc: BP Eric Adams formally approves with 38 recommendations including NYCHA funding and deep affordability.

timeline.label: CPC Votes 9–0
timeline.desc: City Planning Commission votes 9–0 in favor. 50-day City Council window begins.

timeline.label: Brad Lander Leads City Council Approval
timeline.desc: Council Members Brad Lander and Stephen Levin lead the City Council to approve the rezoning. Points of Agreement announced covering NYCHA, affordability, and the Gowanus Oversight Task Force.

timeline.label: Mayor de Blasio Signs Into Law
timeline.desc: Mayor de Blasio signs the Gowanus Neighborhood Plan into law, enacting the rezoning and all Points of Agreement.

poa.name: NYCHA capital investment
poa.text: CB6 made full funding of Gowanus Houses and Wyckoff Gardens a hard condition. The final Points of Agreement committed about $200 million for comprehensive in-unit renovations at both developments.

poa.name: Affordability
poa.text: CB6 demanded deep affordability, 20% of units at 40% AMI. The final agreement went further at Gowanus Green, committing at least 50% of its roughly 950 units at 50% AMI or below.

poa.name: Combined sewer overflow
poa.text: CB6 required the Unified Stormwater Rule, stricter on-site rainwater standards, to be in effect before any new building in the rezoning area could connect to the sewer. The final agreement committed to exactly that.

poa.name: Gowanus Waterfront BID
poa.text: CB6 demanded a Parks Improvement District to fund waterfront maintenance independent of the Parks budget. The final agreement created the Gowanus Waterfront BID for that purpose.

poa.name: Gowanus Oversight Task Force
poa.text: CB6's first and hardest condition was an independent oversight body with real teeth. The final agreement created the Task Force on those terms: quarterly public meetings, senior agency participation, and a mandate through 2037. It has been meeting since December 2021.

oversight.name: Gowanus Improvement District
oversight.text: The effort to form a Business Improvement District covering the rezoning area. A BID is funded by an assessment on property owners and spends it on sanitation, public safety, streetscape and marketing inside its boundary.

oversight.name: Gowanus Oversight Task Force
oversight.text: Tracks the 56 Points of Agreement from the 2021 Gowanus rezoning and publishes Task Force materials. CB6 pushed for a standing oversight body so the commitments made during ULURP would be followed after the vote.

gowanus.environmental_intro: City, state, and federal agencies and community groups working on environmental issues in and around the Gowanus Canal.

environmental.name: NYC DEP, Gowanus Canal
environmental.text: New York City Department of Environmental Protection: CSO work, water quality, and infrastructure around the canal.

environmental.name: NYS DEC, Gowanus Canal Area Sites

environmental.name: US EPA Gowanus CAG

gowanus.ch9_intro: Chapter 9 lays out the rules for the Special Gowanus Mixed Use District, including permitted uses, bulk, parking, streetscape requirements, waterfront access, and special authorizations. It is intended to recognize an existing mixed-use neighborhood, allow compatible residential and light manufacturing uses, improve access to and around the Gowanus Canal, and broaden housing choices and local employment opportunities.

ch9.name: General purposes and definitions
ch9.text: Explains the district's purpose and policy goals. Defines terms such as Gowanus mix uses, Gowanus retail and entertainment uses, and mixed use district. Confirms Chapter 9 controls when it conflicts with other zoning provisions.

ch9.name: Use regulations
ch9.text: Covers permitted uses in manufacturing and mixed-use districts. Includes special categories for Gowanus mix uses and retail and entertainment uses. Adds supplementary rules such as where commercial uses may be located in mixed buildings.

ch9.name: Bulk regulations
ch9.text: Sets floor area rules, including special provisions tied to transit improvements, schools, comfort stations, and street improvements. Includes yard rules, waterfront yards, and height and setback rules by subdistrict. Contains special street wall articulation requirements.

ch9.name: Parking, loading, and curb cuts
ch9.text: Provides special accessory off-street parking regulations. Includes rules for off-site parking and joint facilities. Also covers loading and curb cut regulations.

ch9.name: District plan elements
ch9.text: Includes streetscape regulations, street tree requirements, sidewalk widening, bridge connections, and waterfront public access area requirements. Also includes certifications and authorizations for transit improvements, sites containing schools, and large mixed-use sites.

ch9.name: Gowanus Canal waterfront access plan
ch9.text: Includes area-wide modifications and special public access provisions for specific parcels. Sets special design standards for guardrails, seating, lighting, planting, and paving. Adds signage, maintenance, and operation requirements.
